standard.title: Create Historical Descriptions, Explanations and Arguments
standard.description: create descriptions, explanations and historical arguments, using historical knowledge, concepts and terms
standard.prior_knowledge: In Year 7 students created descriptions, explanations and historical arguments using knowledge and concepts (AC9HH7S08). In Year 8 they continued this (AC9HH8S08). Y9 adds two significant extensions: developing arguments that identify different interpretive possibilities and argue a particular point of view, and selecting appropriate communication formats. Students must now produce genuinely argumentative historical writing, not only explanations.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students create descriptions, explanations and historical arguments that engage with interpretive possibilities, argue a point of view with evidence, and are communicated in appropriate formats.

nodes.label: Developing a historical argument that acknowledges interpretation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can develop a historical argument that identifies different possibilities in interpretation and argues a particular point of view with consistent reference to evidence.
nodes.minimum_width: Write a historical argument that takes a clear position on a historical question and supports it with at least two pieces of evidence.
nodes.typical_width: Develop a historical argument that identifies different possibilities in interpretation and argues a particular point of view with consistent reference to evidence; use historical concepts and terms (cause, significance, change, continuity, perspective) in the argument; demonstrate that a historical argument acknowledges countervailing evidence or interpretations rather than ignoring them.
wider: Develop a historical argument that explicitly addresses a contested interpretation — engaging with a counterargument and explaining why the evidence better supports one interpretation over another

Produce a historical argument drawing on sources representing multiple perspectives (coloniser and colonised, majority and minority) and reflecting explicitly on how source selection shapes the argument

Construct a historical argument that uses both quantitative evidence (data, statistics) and qualitative evidence (primary source quotations, historian's accounts) — demonstrating the integration of different evidence types in argumentation
nodes.hinge_reason: Developing a historical argument that acknowledges interpretive possibilities — rather than simply asserting a position — is the defining advance at Year 9. Students who produce assertion-only arguments without engaging with countervailing evidence or interpretations are not meeting the descriptor's full demand.

response_modes.reason: The shift from explanation to argumentation that acknowledges interpretation requires explicit modelling. Students need to see what it looks like to acknowledge a counterargument before they can produce this themselves. Model the structure: 'While some historians argue X, the evidence better supports Y because...'

success_criteria: Develops a historical argument that takes a clear position and supports it with at least two pieces of evidence
Acknowledges at least one alternative interpretation or piece of countervailing evidence, and explains why the argument's position is better supported

nodes.label: Selecting appropriate formats and using historical concepts and terms
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can select appropriate formats to communicate a historical argument and use historical concepts and terms accurately throughout.
nodes.minimum_width: Communicate a historical argument in an appropriate format, using at least three historical terms or concepts correctly.
nodes.typical_width: Select appropriate formats to communicate a historical argument — including written essays, oral presentations, scripts, visual displays, or structured reports; develop explanations and arguments using historical concepts and terms such as cause, effect, change, continuity, significance, perspective, and contested historical interpretations; construct historical arguments using selected evidence from sources.
wider: Construct a historical argument in an unfamiliar format (e.g. a museum exhibit text, a podcast script, a documentary treatment) — adapting historical reasoning to a specific audience and purpose

Develop historical arguments across multiple formats within the same unit (e.g. a written essay and an oral presentation on related but distinct questions) — practising the skill of adapting argument to communication context

Produce a historical argument for a non-specialist audience (e.g. a Year 7 student or a community website) — examining how communicating history to different audiences requires different choices about language, structure, and level of detail

response_modes.reason: Practising historical argument construction across multiple formats — written, oral, visual — and multiple audiences develops the skill as genuinely communicative rather than a formula for one output type.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Historical argument in diverse formats — essays, oral presentations, scripts, museum text — develops students' capacity to communicate historical reasoning to different audiences. This is both an assessment skill and a genuine literacy skill with application beyond the history classroom.
success_criteria: Communicates a historical argument in a format appropriate to the audience and purpose, with accurate use of at least three historical terms or concepts
Constructs the argument using selected evidence from sources, not only general claims
